18.2.Kick Indicators/Warning Signs

Primary well control warning signs and early detection is paramount to identify that an alert condition results, i.e. that a kick may be developing! Every endeavor then taken by all personnel to assure the following well control risks are managed as low as reasonably practicable e.g.

• Positive gain in the active mud pit volume

• In sufficient hole-fill or returns volumes of fluids during tripping

• Increased flow from annulus

• Decrease in pump pressure

• Loss Circulation

• Losses and gains to/from the wellbore

• Rapid increase in penetration rate (drilling break)

• Decrease in penetration rate (inverse drilling break PDC enters a sand)

• Gas cut mud and/or increase in chloride content in mud

• Swabbing, especially the "low volume swabbing" and the dangerous effect of migrating and

expanding gas

• Unexpected increased readings on gas-chromatograph

• Trip gas and increased trip gas during sub-sequent round trips

• Connection gas

• Pressure caving’s appear on shakers

• Increasing pump strokes, ROP, torque and drag trends all indicating pore pressure may be

increasing

• Flowline temperature increases

When these warning signs occur, an alert condition exists. Immediate action must then be taken to assure that well control risks can be safely managed at the lowest risk.

18.4.Well Control Procedure in Summary

Personnel

It is required that each member of crew should be familiar with every item of equipment used in well control. The minimum personal knowledge and capability required for a crew member to be considered competent are:

• To have sufficient knowledge of all the equipment in order to be able to determine when

operating functions are not working properly, and consequently, take all necessary remedial

actions to re-instate full functionality.

• To have sufficient knowledge of operating procedures in order to be able to react in time,

understanding completely what is occurring.

• To be able to correctly interpret the various abnormal situations and take the appropriate

remedial steps of action. Carry out basic calculations, and use the results in order to safely manage

any occurrences.

Key personnel shall have the fundamental theoretical knowledge on kick and blow-out control techniques and also hold a current Well Control Certificate issued by an accredited industry training institute recognized by Governmental bodies and operators.

Recordings

All BOP test, drills, function test, any malfunction, repair or maintenance to the mud system and well control equipment shall be recorded in the IADC daily reports and shall be signed by both the Drilling Contractor's Tool Pusher and Drilling Supervisor on the well site. They shall also be recorded in the PECO Daily Drilling Report.

Flow Check Procedure

To avoid a kick situation, it is recommended that a flow check be conducted at specific times during the drilling operation.

1. While drilling (any warning sign)

2. Prior to tripping the drill string

3. While out of hole (continuously)

4. While tripping (any warning sign)

Trip out:

• After pulling 5% of the drill pipe

• At the midpoint depth of the wellbore

• Prior to pulling the first stand of drill collars

• After all the drill string is out of hole.

Trip in:

• Upon reaching surface casing shoe

• At midpoint of the wellbore

Killing Well Method and Shut-In Method

• Driller's method is recommended main killing methods for the project.

• The hard shut-in method is recommended to minimize influx.

Sepehr-Jufair Field Development and Production

Operations Project

Well Drilling Program - JR-09

Doc. No: SJD4 DDRGED DRDR PLDR 9001 D01 Page 277 of 281

Kick detection and Hard Shut in Procedure While Drilling

• Kick detection procedure:

If there is an indication of a possible kick occurring, the driller shall follow the kick detection procedures outlined below.

a) Stop drilling, pick up drill pipe to a predetermined Space-out position with pump on.

b) Shut off pump and check for well flow by visual examination on the bell nipple, flow line and mud pit.

If the well is not flowing to be confirmed:

Immediately notify the drilling supervisor and toolpusher.

The Drilling Supervisor will decide whether to circulate bottoms up or resume drilling. The penetration rate will be limited as long as the cause of the abnormal situation is undetermined. Always be aware that some hydrocarbons (gas or oil cut mud) may rise to the surface. Ensure that the proper monitoring and safety systems all in place.

If the well is flowing to be confirmed:

Close the well as per the Hard Shut-in Procedure.

• Hard Shut-in Procedure

a) Space kelly (if in use) and/or tool joint so that tool joints are clear of sealing elements.

b) Pump off and flow check.

c) If a kick is confirmed, sound alarm.

d) Close annular preventer and open remote controlled choke line valve (HCR).

e) If the well has been closed using the annular preventer, check space out (pipe rams vs. toll joint

relative position) and close pipe rams and ram locks

f) Bleed off pressure between pipe rams and annular preventer (if possible).

g) Record shut-in drill pipe pressure and shut-in casing pressures.

h) Record volume gain and mark pits.

i) Check mud weight for in and out.

j) Check blowout preventer and manifold for leaks.

k) Check flowline and choke exhaust for flow.

l) Check accumulator pressure.

Kick Detection and Hard Shut in Procedure while Tripping

• Kick Detection Procedure

If there is an indication of a possible kick occurring, the driller shall follow the kick detection procedures outlined below.

a) Stop tripping; slack off string to a predetermined space-out position.

b) Install a fully open safety valve and hand tight on drill pipe/work string. Close the safety valve.

c) Check for well flow by visual examination on the bell nipple, flow line and mud pit.

If the well is not flowing to be confirmed:

Resume tripping with extreme care.

If the well is flowing to be confirmed:

Close the well as per the Hard Shut-In Procedure

Sepehr-Jufair Field Development and Production

Operations Project

Well Drilling Program - JR-09

Doc. No: SJD4 DDRGED DRDR PLDR 9001 D01 Page 278 of 281

• Hard Shut-in Procedure

a) If a kick is confirmed, sound alarm.

b) Install full opened safety valve on drill string and close same.

c) Space tool joints clear of sealing elements and close annular preventer. Open remote controlled

choke line valve (HCR).

d) Make up kelly or top drive (Add a pup joint or single between safety valve and top drive). Open

safety valve.

e) Record shut-in drill pipe pressure and shut-in casing pressures.

f) Check blowout preventer, stack, and manifold for leaks. Check valves status on well control

system. Check accumulator pressure.

g) Check mud weight for in and out..

h) Manage to strip to bottom.

Kick Detection and Hard Shut in Procedure while Out of Hole

• Kick Detection Procedure

If there is an indication of a possible kick occurring, the driller shall follow the kick detection procedures outlined below.

a) Stop working immediately.

b) Check for well flowing by visual examination on the bell nipple, flow line and mud pit.

If the well is not flowing to be confirmed:

Resume working and continuously monitoring well.

If the well is flowing to be confirmed:

Close the well as per the ‗Hard Shut-In Procedure‘

• Hard Shut-in Procedure

a) Manage to RIH with drill pipe as more as possible if hole condition permits, and the drill pipe must

be installed a full opening safety valve (stabbing valve).

b) Close the annular preventer and open remote controlled choke line valve (HCR).

c) If the well has been closed using the annular preventer, check space out (pipe rams vs. toll joint

relative position) and close pipe rams and ram locks.

d) Bleed off pressure between pipe rams and annular preventer (if possible).

e) Record shut-in drill pipe pressure and shut-in casing pressures.

Well Control During Running Casing

The well control while running casing is important and critical, best practices shall be followed, including but not limited to:

Change out pipe size rams with casing size rams prior to running casing for expected hydrocarbon bearing formation, if possible except running a liner string with drill pipe.

The crossover for casing connection to drill pipe must available on floor. A good practice is to keep a joint of DP with casing crossover at lower end and full opened safety valve at upper end to be ready for picking up on V-door.

Shut in procedure during logging

Recover logging tools as possible when a kick is suspected during logging. If pit gain exceeds the specified amount, Wire line should be cut immediately. Sound alarm and shut in well as procedure for empty wells. Recover cable through closed annular preventer is not recommended.

1. General Information

1.1 Field Introduction

Azadegan South Oil Field is situated in West Karoun province on a large long-axis anticline with N-S trending with approximate dimensions about 20 km width and 60 km length near to Iran-Iraq border, to the east of Yaran Oil Field.

The trap area of the south Azadegan is limited to 43.2x17.2 km. The Azadegan Oil field was discovered in 1999, when Well AZN-1 was drilled vertically down to the Cretaceous Fahliyan Formation with total depth of 4,643 m. The results of this well, revealed the reservoir characteristics of the field. Following to the result of the well no. AZN-1, another 5 exploration wells was drilled in different parts of this huge field down to Fahliyan Formation. In the later stage the well No.10 assumed as exploration well for evaluation of deeper formations. This well was drilled in 2008, down to the depth of 5340m (Neyriz Fm.), mainly to evaluate the Jurassic formations.

Based on the exploration wells results, carbonate reservoir of Sarvak Formation is broadly developed in Azadegan Field. This formation was penetrated in all of seven exploration wells (AZN-1, AZN-2, AZN- 3, AZN-4, AZN-5, AZN-6 and AZN-10). Clastic oil-bearing zones of Kazhdumi Formation developed in main anticline of Azadegan Field, extending from north to center of South Azadegan. The Clastic oilbearing zones of Gadvan Formation developed only in crest area and south parts of South Azadegan Filed, which was discovered by AZN-1 in crest and AZN-4 in south parts. The carbonates of Fahliyan Formation also developed in Azadegan field, but the oil reservoir of this formation developed in South part of South Azadegan.

The Azadegan Field is an elongated anticline, trending in N-S direction, belonging to "Arabian Trend".

The stratigraphy sequence of the field includes AghaJari, Gachsaran, Asmari, Fahliyan, Pabdeh, Gurpi, Ilam, Laffan, Sarvak, Kazhdumi, Dariyan, Gadvan and Fahliyan Formations, from top to bottom. This sequence in well no AZN-10, the deepest up to now drilled well of the field, continues with Garau, Gotnia, Najmah, Sargalu, Alan, Mus and Neyriz formations.

The Dominant lithofacies of Sarvak Formation are Rudist-bearing packstone and partially grainstone, which contains abundant bioclasts. Some other facies like matrix-dominated wackestone and mudstone are also found.

The AZADEGAN Oilfield is located in Khuzestan province and is approximately located 80 Kilometers West of Ahwaz City, near to Iran-Iraq Border. It is in the Northwest of the YADAVARAN Field and in the West of JUFEYR Field. the average monthly Temperature is 45ºc in summer, and highest

1.4 Reservoir Information

1.4.1 Key Reservoir Descriptions

Fahliyan Formation: This carbonate to argillaceous carbonate Formation is limited by overlying thick argillaceous successions in the upper part (eaquivalent to the Iraqi Ratawi Formation) and the main part consists of different bioclastic limestones with some layers of shale and argillaceous facies that can be assumed equivalent with Iraqi Yamama Formation. However, in South Azadegan wells 1, 2 and 5 the Fahliyan Formation is characterized by fossiliferous limestone beds and interbedded shales. It should be noted that most of Majnoon wells penetrated into the Sarvak and Fahliyan carbonates as one of the main reservoir targets.

1.5.1 Expected Stratigraphy and Formation Top in F-20

The area is completely covered by the alluvium of Holocene age; the drilled will be Aghajari, Gachsaran, Asmari, Pabdeh, Gurpi, Ilam, Laffan, Sarvak, Kazhdumi, Dariyan, Gadvan and Fahliyan formations. A brief stratigraphic sequence has been predicted as follows:

- Aghajari Formation (surface to 1021mMD) (Drilled Thickness: 1021 m)

The Aghajari Formation consists of a repetition of brown to grey calcareous sandstones, chert debris and gypsum-veined red marl. A fauna of brackish to freshwater was observed, together with more marine fauna.. Aghajari overlays Gachsaran Formation with a conformable boundary.

- Gachsaran Formation (1021-1368 mMD) (Drilled Thickness: 347m)

The Gachsaran Formation with a thickness ranges from 400 m to 500 m thickens towards the north. Deposition of the Gachsaran Formation is cyclic. The cycle began with a deposition of shallow-water marine carbonates, and then it was overlain by a thick evaporitic phase. The evaporates were capped by red to variegated marl, which represented the end of cycle. Gachsaran is laid on Asmari Formation with a comformable boundary.

- Asmari Formation (1368-1583 mMD) (Drilled Thickness: 215 m)

The Asmari Formation in Azadegan Field developed a massive sandstone interval, with a few thin argillaceous limestones in the upper sections. Sandstone are clear, fine to medium-sorted, and poorly consolidated. On the other hand, the lower sections consist of intercalation of sandy, chalky, slightly dolomitic high-energy limestone with sandstone layers. Asmari is parallel to Pabdeh Formation at the bottom.

- Pabdeh Formation (1994-2178 mMD) (Drilled Thickness: 165 m)

Pabdeh Formation is divided into two parts in the Azadegan field. The upper part is made of grey to dark-brown argillaceous limestones and marls. Planktonic fauna dates that this part was deposited in Oligocene. The lower part is composed of dark-brown, slightly argillaceous limestone. Pelagic fauna, mostly Globigerina and Globorotalia, indicates that this part was formed during late Paleocene to late Eocene in age. It seems that no early Paleocene Formation exists in the Azadegan area. Chert and cherty limestone layers at the bottom of Pabdeh Formation are very important for drilling parameters on the PDC bit (as a notification for drilling operation department).

- Gurpi Formation (2178-2560mMD) (Drilled Thickness: 382 m)

Gurpi Formation consists of argillaceous limestone with higher clay content rather than Pabdeh Formation. About 50 meters of pure limestone will be observed in the middle part of the formation which divides it into 3 different parts as below:

Type of Completion 7” Cemented Liner (Production through Perforation)Nearby Wells AZNS-070-ST2, AZNS-049, AZNS-173 (Gadvan target)

- Upper Gurpi (2178-2343mMD) (Drilled Thickness: 165 m)

The Gurpi Formation in the Azadegan Field consists of grey to dark-brownish, slightly argillaceous micritic limestone with Maestrichtian to Campanian aged fauna. At Well AZN-01, about 50 meters of chalky limestones were encountered in the middle of the Gurpi formation, which contains abundant fragments of rudists, bryozoa, corals, and Orbitoides.

- Tarbur Member (2343-2418 mMD) (Drilled Thickness: 75 m)

In the western Abadan Plain about 50 meters thick chalky limestone was encountered in the middle part of the Gurpi Formation, which contains abundant fragments of bioclasts, suggesting very shallow depositional environment. This interval is equivalnt to the Tarbur Formation with reservoir quality in other regions.

- Lower Gurpi (2418-2560 mMD) (Drilled Thickness: 142 m)

This member consists of gray, light gray, medium hard argillaceous Limestone. The Gurpi formation is overlain directly on Ilam formation by conformity contact.

- Ilam Formation (2560-2629 mMD) (Drilled Thickness: 69 m)

In the Azadegan Field, the Ilam Formation consists of grey micritic limestone, often argillaceous, rarely pyritic, limestones. Microfauna, mostly pelagic, including rotalids and oligostegina assemblage, a few algae, bryozoa, and rudist fragments exist.

- Laffan Member (2629-2635mMD) (Drilled Thickness: 6 m)

The Laffan Formation developed a thin greenish-grey pyritic shale layer with ostracods fauna that capping the Sarvak Formation.

- Sarvak Formation (2635-3270 mMD) (Drilled Thickness: 635 m)

The Sarvak Formation developed a carbonate unit, which was gradually overlying the Kazhdumi Formation, and it is abruptly terminated by an erosion phase, covered by a various late Cretaceous sediment. The lithology of Sarvak consists of the dark grey fine grained nodular argillaceous limestone interbedded with thin marls in the bottom. The Limestone graded upward into a white-to-buff massive chalky limestone with siliceous nodules; developed a very massive tan-to-brown limestone containing abundant rudist debris in the middle part. In the upper part is made up of rubbly limestone with red staining and leached zones of breccia and the top of Sarvak Formation is very ferruginous.

- Kazhdumi Formation (3270-3464 mMD) (Drilled Thickness: 194 m)

Kazhdumi Formation begins with dark brown, soft to medium hard, some fissile and calcareous Shale. This formation is start with dark brown to dark green gray, medium hard to hard, soft to medium, high bituminous, calcareous Shale interbedded with argillaceous limestone, sandy claystone, claystone, marl, sandy limestone, limestone beds. The Argillaceous Limestone is dark brown to brown gray, medium hard to hard, micro bituminous. The Sandy claystone is light green gray, soft, high calcareous. The Claystone is gray to light gray, soft. The Marl is green gray, soft, sticky. The Sandy Limestone is dark green gray, hard, faint sandy. The Limestone is light gray to green gray, medium hard to soft, partly argillaceous. The Kazhdumi Formation at base is consisting of Azadegan Member.

- Dariyan Formation (3464-3622 mMD) (Drilled Thickness: 158 m)

In Dariyan Formation a variety of lithological rock types such as carbonates, rich organic shales and sandstones were deposited in various environments. The lower part of the Gadvan Formation is composed of low-energy, but not very deep, micritic, often argillaceous limestone

with echinoids and algal fragments. Two sandstone units were defined in the Gadvan Formation lateral changes and especially discontinuity of the sandstone layers which are consist of fine clastics (shales and siltstones) may be expected

The Gadvan formation divided to three part:Dariyan formation starts with white to white cream grey clean limestone type I/II, I. Base of Dariyan formation, appears grey, green Pyritic shale interbedded with argillaceous limestone. This zone called transition zone and thickness is 16m. after last grey limestone indicates of Gadvan formation.

This carbonate formation contains three zones. D1 and D3 are non-reservoirs and D2 is a moderately poor reservoir.

- Gadvan Formation (3622-3915 mMD) (Drilled Thickness: 293 m)

In This Formation a variety of lithological rock types such as carbonates, rich organic shales and sandstones were deposited in various environments. The lower part of the Gadvan Formation is composed of low-energy, but not very deep, micritic, often argillaceous limestone with echinoids and algal fragments. Two sandstone units were defined in the Gadvan Formation lateral changes and especially discontinuity of the sandstone layers which are consist of fine clastics (shales and siltstones) may be expected

The Gadvan Formation divided to three part;

Upper Gadvan; the upper part starts with occurrence of a terrigenous rock. The lithology is composed of grey claystone and some shale.

Khalij Mbr.; appears with pure limestone, cream, light brown and in some intervals oil stain.

Lower Gadvan; consisting of alternating of marl, argillaceous limestone, limestone, claystone, sandy claystone and sandstone beds. The Marl is green gray, soft, sticky, slightly calcareous. The Argillaceous Limestone is gray white gray medium hard to soft, partly pyritic. The Limestone is white, white to light gray, hard. The Claystone is light gray, soft, sticky. The Sandy Claystone is light gray, soft, sticky, fine sand grained. The Sandstone is brown to gray, partly white buff, gray, friable, sorted, sub rounded, medium quartz grained, partly calcareous. This sandstone which occur in Zone-3 and Zone-5 are the reservoir of this formation and in this part is equivalent with Kushk member.

- Fahliyan Formation (3915-4180.0 mMD)(TD) (Drilled Thickness: 265m +)

This formation is start with light gray, light green gray, soft Limestone interbedded with green gray, soft, sticky Marl, green gray, light gray, soft, Argillaceous Limestone and dark green gray, soft, sticky Clay stone beds. This formation at continue is consisting of buff white light gray, light brown, brown, medium hard, hard, densely, slightly argillaceous Limestone and off white, white gray, medium hard Chalky Limestone beds.

2) Other requirements for Wellbore Quality

 Average borehole diameter enlargement rate less than 15%

 All casing/liner are run to designed depth (normally 1-2m above TD/section TD)

 No fills at bottom of hole

 No junk lost in hole

 No abnormal casing wear and casing deformation caused by CONTRACTOR’s malpractice

3) Well trajectory control key points

 Drill upper formation before KOP using Pendulum BHA, low WOB and high RPM, to ensure vertical hole drilled.

 Control the distance between two holes in one well pad is not less than 2 meters. Single-shot and multi-shot will be

used to monitor the well trajectory. Take single shot survey at interval of 100m; run multi-shot survey each 300m

from surface to kick off point. If necessary, survey shall be run more frequently.

 Run build up BHA (Motor + MWD) whenever collision risk increases to build up a little inclination (2~4°) and

bottom hole departure to avoid collision at vertical section if necessary.

 If magnetic interference exists, gyroscopic inclinometer shall be used in order to avoid collision.

 Amend the planned profile according to the data obtained by electronic multi-shot or single-shot survey in vertical

hole, and locate the kick off point.

 MWD/GR will be used in directional drilling to ensure that the actual well path will coincide with the planned well trajectory to the

extent that it shall not pass through the boundaries of the corridor that surrounds the planned hole trajectory in case a corridor has

been specified.

 LWD/GR will be utilized in horizontal drilling in order to controlling well trajectory, especially in Sarvak-3.

 The downhole motor and MWD shall be used in vertical hole section if necessary.

 Monitors and analyses the build-up ability of the BHA used in directional/horizontal section. Due to the lagged survey data

measured by MWD, inclination, azimuth and the buildup rate should be predicted based on the instant survey at all times. If

necessary, more surveys should be taken so as to adjust drilling parameters and BHA, control the well trajectory within the

specified target tolerance strictly.

 In buildup section, to avoid pipe-stuck, BHA should be designing such way to minimize sliding mode time especially in clay

formations. To reduce torque in rotating mode and consequently reduce sliding mode time, using stabilizer with short gauge and

profile.

 Using circulating sub above MWD is recommended due to sever loss in this area.

 Adjust the drilling method according to the well survey data, and control the change amplitude of inclination and azimuth to ensure

the smoothness of the well trajectory.

 In this section, the torque and drag are relatively higher, torque and drag analysis for each BHA run should be performed, and

torque and drag reduction measures (for example simplifying the BHA or running cuttings bed impeller) are recommended.

P/U &amp;amp; M/U 26" bit #1 (R.Bit) and 9-3/4" drill collars, RIH to tag formation @ ±14m.

Drilling 26" hole from 14 to 150m (20" casing point in Aghajari formation) using Hi-vis

bentonite pill (Run Totco each 50m).

Perform hole condition prior to run casing. If observe any indication of drag, run back to

bottom, POOH to surface.

R/U casing running equipment &amp;amp; run 150 m approximately 13 Jts. 20" casing to 150 m.Fill

casing by non-LCM fresh mud.

3. Sequence of Drilling Operation

3.1 Rig Move

 Hold pre-move meeting on location. Discuss contingency plans for:

Safe arrangements for rig up and rig down.

Safe standby areas for rig

In case move have to be suspended.

Loss of trucks in case of repair.

Moving at night.

 Hold pre-move safety meeting. Ensure everyone understands individual responsibilities:

 Commence rigging down. The ordering of trucks will be done by rig manager.

 Commence rig move to F20, PAD NO. 93

Position rig for optimal operations

 Rig up on cellar

Rig up and commence operational procedure for (F20)

Before leaving previous location, all equipment should be checked.

 Test all manifold and surface safety valves

RKB – GLE and Elevation

Spud date and time.

 Mud tanks should be empty during move. After moving Fill water tanks and keep as full as possible.

3.2 Pre Spud

3.2.1 Certificate

 All rig equipment is on location, properly rigged up and function-tested. Check availability and content of hoisting

equipment inspection &amp;amp; maintenance records according to API.

 All rig equipment including all Tubulars, Subs, Tools &amp;amp; … should be inspected &amp;amp; according to API.

3.2.2 Safety Device

 Test draw-works crown block saver and record results on daily drilling report; test derrick man escape device

(Geronimo line) and record time required for test weight on daily drilling report; test rig intercom system, especially

for Driller-Derrick Man and Driller-Mud Logger communication link.

 Check that all rig safety equipment, e.g., fire extinguishers, eye-wash stations etc., is installed at the proper locations

as per rig layout diagrams.

 Verify that substructure is level and foundation adequate to support drilling unit during whole well period and that

mast is centered above rotary table.

 Ensure rig alignment with Top Drive System. Make sure rig tongs and rig floor hoisting equipment are adequate for

handling 8-1/2″ and 9-1/2″ drill collars. Make sure that mechanical tong torque gauges for drill pipe/drill collar are

properly functioning and have been calibrated; re-calibrated as required.

South Azadegan Oilfield Project

Contract No:

F – 20 Well Drilling Program Page 49 of 181

3.2.3 Rig Equipment

 Verify that the 26″ tri-cone bit is ready to be picked up, all nozzles installed, and 26″ bit breakers are on the rig floor.

Make sure single-shot or multi-shot survey tools available for vertical section survey.

 Make sure all solids control equipment are correctly installed and have been function-tested with charging pressure

gauges in place where applicable. Make sure adequate screen inventory for the shale shakers is available in the sizes

required for the well. Make sure water tanks are completely filled and transfer lines from water tanks to mud system

are hooked up. Make sure all mud materials and chemicals required to drill 26″ section is on location, in sound

condition and suitably stored. Make sure that bentonite is pre-hydrated and sufficient volume has been built for top

section and for well-kill.

 Make sure that all mud pumps have been fitted with new consumable parts: liners, pistons, valves, seats etc. Make

sure that pulsation dampeners are charged with Nitrogen to the proper pre-charge pressure, 30% of expected

standpipe pressure during drilling of the 26″ hole section; check if sufficient Nitrogen bottles are available on

location to adjust pulsation dampener pre-charge pressure as required. Make sure that mud pump pop-off valves are

set at the proper pressure for the liner sizes installed and that the mud discharge lines from the pop-off valves to the

mud tanks are properly secured. Check that all high-pressure hoses are properly secured with safety chains. P/T

should be done to high-pressure surface line of circulating system.

3.2.4 Wellhead &amp;amp; BOP

 Have 2″ line pipe nipple with 2″ ball valve welded to 30″ conductor pipe 0.2m above cellar bottom to drain cement

from conductor/riser pipe after cementing 20″ surface casing. Verify that pre-installed 30″ conductor pipe is vertical

and that no angle/bend exists between conductor and 30″ riser pipe.

 Make sure that adequate supply of 20″ casing is on location, inspected and ready to be run, float shoe should already

be made up, centralizers should be pre-installed on the pipe-rack prior to spud in the well.

 Ensure mud logging unit is functioning and equipment are calibrated and tested properly.

3.2.5 Others

 Verify that the rig’s fuel tanks are full to meet minimum of three days rig consumption available on site.

 Make sure all waste treatment equipment available and commissioning test is ok.

 Hold pre-spud meeting with relevant service Company personnel on location. Discuss procedures involved

throughout 26″ hole section drilling, reporting system and critical safety operation measures.

 OEOC prepared a pre-spud checklist and distributed it in rigs. The checklist will be performed based on the

aforementioned checklist. In addition to the checklist, following matters should be checked:

 Check &amp;amp; observe the alignment of the rig. This check will be performed in four stages; rig levelling, derrick

verticality, derrick alignment with rotary table, rotary table alignment with conductor pipe. To do this pick up 3 joints

of 9 3/4" DC and check the verticality of the derrick.

 Mechanical facilities for mud treatment such as:

1. Desander, Desilter, (Degasser, mud centrifuge), mud cleaner, proper size of shaker–screens, hoppers, mud guns &amp;amp; mixers, should be all available on rig and functioning properly.

2. All mud tanks, mud transfer lines &amp;amp; connection should be checked by filling them with water &amp;amp; cross wellhead circulation.

3. Mud engineer laboratory should be equipped with a complete set of testing equipment. The calibration should be done under supervision of well site drilling supervisor before starting the operation.

4. Weight indicator, rotary speed gauge, any smart drilling instrumentation, Top Drive, Stroke meter, pressure gauges on manifold and in the drilling console, loss / gain gauge and any other gauges should be checked and calibrated.

5. (Grand manifold valves &amp;amp; related lines), Stand pipe manifold (lines) valves &amp;amp; connection must be checked &amp;amp; pressure tested.

6. All motors, (SCR &amp;amp; VFD) should be checked under load prior to start drilling.

7. Check &amp;amp; control mud stock &amp;amp; cement stock every day &amp;amp; if there is any necessity to request mud material, cement or any drilling tool, it should be prepared &amp;amp; requested at proper time.

 Pre-spud check list

3.3 Drilling

3.3.1 26” Hole Section, 20” Casing

After commencing spud-in, 26” hole drilling will be started. The drilling would be anticipated to go on fast.

Casing Point 20” Casing @ 150 mMDFormation AghajariRisks &amp;amp; Hole problems Bit balled upDeviation control INCLINOMETER (TOTCO)Logging ---Bit Type R. Bit (1-1-5)Drilling FluidPre-Hydrated Bentonite mudMW 65-67PV 5-18 CPVis. &amp;gt;50Drilling ParametersWOB 10-30GPM 900-1000RPM Max available

3.3.1.1 Sequence of Operation

 Make up 26” BHA as per BHA design. Tag formation at ±14m.

 Drill ahead formation down to 150 m (20” casing point in Aghajari formation) using Hi-vis bentonite pill. (pump HiVis Pill Periodically) Pay enough attention to drill straight hole.

Note:

In Case of complete loss while drilling 26” hole Cure by pump LCM pill or cement as cement plug.

 TD should be adjusted to have 1m of rat hole below casing shoe.

 The exact TD will be determined based on casing tally.

 Run Inclinometer (Totco) each 50m to evaluate the verticality of the hole.

 Ensure that all drilling tools and equipment are on well site and are in serviceable condition.

 Ensure that adequate fishing tools for this section of hole are available.

 Enough Mud Material, LCM and cement should be available on rig site to use in case of needing.

South Azadegan Oilfield Project

Contract No:

F – 20 Well Drilling Program Page 51 of 181

 At TD, Circulate and clean the hole. Spot high viscosity pill at bottom, drop Inclinometer (Totco) POOH to surface.

Check Bit.

 Perform hole condition prior to run casing. If observe any indication of drag, run back to bottom. Wash and ream to

make sure that the hole condition is good.

 Perform safety meeting.

 R/U casing running equipment.

 Run ±150m (Approx. 13 Jts) 20", 94 ppf, K-55, BTC casing with stab-in duplex shoe to bottom as per casing

program. (function test of F.shoe should be checked on surface by WSS). Casing shoe should be adjusted to have 1m

of rat hole and enough stick up (1 m on rig floor). Fill casing by non-LCM fresh mud.

Note:

 Take care when running casing not to set down excessive weight if tight hole or ledges are encountered.

 Run stinger on DP’s using the “C” Plate &amp;amp; 5” x 20” centralizer. Sting in. M/U &amp;amp; test cementing lines. Circulate for

one casing annulus volume. While circulating, check the DPs annulus for any return. Use all DPs weight on the string

if observing any minor leakage through DPs annulus.

 Cement casing as per program. Any minor adjustment regarding the corrected depth will be done in due time.

Displace with mud (1-2 bbls Short Displace). Monitor for pressures. Record and report the final pressure, Sting out.

Check the float. POOH one stand, Circulate to flush/clean drill pipe.

 After cement returns to cellar floor, open the 2" nipple on conductor &amp;amp; flush it.

 POOH to surface. L/D stinger.

 Keep the casing on the elevator until cement surface samples get hard. Check for casing to be center inside conductor

pipe.

Note:

 Based on the results obtained from cementing, decision will be made to perform top jobs.

 If there is no cement return to surface, a top job should be performed to fill the annulus. Use same slurry weight as

the primary cement slurry. Ensure the availability of adequate X-over for connecting line pipe to cement line. The

cement should be accelerated with max. (2%) Calcium Chloride BWOC and no other additives. Wait for the top job

cement to get hard.

 Check casing by slack off weight.

 Cut conductor pipe. Rough cut landing joint and L/D C.P. and L.J. Dress and bevel 20” suitable to install and to weld

casing head housing.

 Install and weld Casing Head Housing 20 ¾” – 3000 psi on casing and pressure test the sealing of welded casing.

(Limit pressure to a maximum of 80% of the collapse strength of the casing, recommended testing pressure: 400 psi).

Outlets must be aligning with cellar stairs.

 Before installing the casing head housing, open all the test ports and clean inside it with water and air.

 Check the 20 ¾” wear bushing, 20 ¾” Plug Tester and 13-3/8” Casing Slip and seal assembly in CHH before

installing CHH (on Surface).

 N/U 21 ¼”-3000 BOP stack and related lines and valves and test all to 2400psi.

 N/U Bell Nipple &amp;amp; flow line

 P/U &amp;amp; M/U Next BHA and stand drill pipes to 2182m.

Casing Tally

BHA reports

Bit Reports

Casing Report

Cement Report

3.3.2.2 Formation Sampling

Every 10 meters a sample would be to section TD.

NOTE: In addition to this general rule, geologist may decide to take more samples.

3.3.2.3 Sequence of Operation

 Make up 17-1/2” BHA as per BHA Design. RIH, tag top of cement, Drill out cement &amp;amp; shoe and rat hole cement.

Work on junk sub.

 Watch carefully for any indication of abnormal torque, since there might be a possibility of shoe being backed off.

Report problem immediately.

 Continue drilling 3m below shoe. Clean out the rat hole, circulate clean.

 Drill ahead formation down to 25m below 20” casing shoe with hi-vis pill. (Pump Hi-Vis pill Periodically)

Note:

If use stabilizer to drill out shoe track, make sure the RPM &amp;amp; WOB are in low as possible until the stabilizer is out from shoe Then Cont. Drilling 17-1/2” hole section with same BHA.

 Circulate and clean hole, POOH to surface and P/U the same bit &amp;amp; S. Stab @ 20m according to BHA program, RIH

to bottom.

 Drill ahead 17-1/2” hole section down to 750 m. CBU.

 Condition trip to 150m, run back and displace mud in hole by 74 pcf KCL/Polymer.

 Continue drilling to 850m or End of Bit Life, circ to clean hole, POOH to surface.

 P/U new PDC bit and Drill ahead 17-1/2” hole section down to 1750 m, 5m meanwhile perform condition trip each

300 m. If observe Chert particle while formation sampling, Follow Contingency Plan#01

 Cont. Drill ahead 17-1/2” hole section down to casing point @ ±2182m, 5m TVD below top of Gurpi formation

meanwhile perform condition trip each 300 m.

Note: In case of observe Cherty zone (Pabdeh formation), Stop Drilling, circulate to clean the hole, POOH to surface and change PDC bit by Tri Cone Bit.

Note:

 For this well Single-shot every 100m and multi-shot survey every 300m to Control Well Deviation or take gyro shot

(5-6 shots each 500-600m)

 Adjust mud weight according to program and as hole condition dictate.

 Tight holes, minor stucks and bit balling are hole problems which happen in offset wells.

 TD should be adjusted in such a way to have 1 meters of rat hole for probable fillings, before running casing.

 Choke manifold and choke line must be lined up for SOFT SHUT-IN through pit or burning line.

 Ensure that adequate fishing tools for this section are available.

 Ensure that enough amount and type of LCM are available and keep ready to mix and pump LCM Pills to cure

losses.

 At section TD, circulate, clean hole. Perform wiper condition trip to shoe and observe well @ shoe. RIH (back to

BTM, check for any drag, CBU), Check for any fill. CBU on bottom. Spot 100 bbl. hi-vis pill @ bottom. POOH to

surface

 If observed any indication of tight hole, run back to TD. W&amp;amp;R to make sure that the hole condition is good prior to

run Log.

 Rig up Wireline logging equipment and run CDR/GR /CAL log as per program, POOH and L/D log

 Perform pre-job safety meeting. R/U casing running equipment. Run casing 68#, N-80, BTC with F. shoe below first

joint &amp;amp; F. collar as per casing program (function test of F. shoe &amp;amp; F. Collar should be checked on surface) while

Circ. BTM’s up at shoe with low GPM.

 Rig pump efficiency should be check in trip-tank before cement job.

 Casing shoe depth should be adjusted in such a way to have 1 meters of rat hole and enough stick up (1.5 m) on rig

floor.

 When casing is at casing setting depth circulate while preparing for cementing M/U &amp;amp; test cementing lines. Circulate

for 120% of casing annulus volume.

 Cement casing as per program. Any minor adjustment regarding the corrected depth will be done in due time.

Displace with mud. Monitor for pressures.

 Bump plug with 1500 psi (Max 80% Casing Burst) / 15 min as CIT (In case of not observing bumping during CMT

job, perform CIT W/1500psi (Max 80% of 13-3/8” Casing Burst)/15min with consider mud weight after D/O CMT

7m above F. Shoe also consider MW while perform CIT), Record and report the final pressure, Bleed off pressure,

3.3.3.3 Sequence of Operations

test with 1500 psi/15min) drill out cement and shoe track (while RIH pick up and rack back 500m 5"DP.)

Note: if shoe and float collar are PDC drillable, use PDC bit with stabilizer at first trip without junk sub and take care while drill shoe track to avoid bit damage.

3.3.4.5 Well Flowing

 The main objectives of the 96 hrs clean up and well flowing is to displace completion fluid, possible mud losses, and

flow back the reservoir fluid until achieving the clean up operation criteria. The clean up operation procedure by rig

is categorized as follows:

 Rigging up all related-equipment and perform hydro-test

 Retrieving barriers (plug, TWV) and landing protection sleeve in TRSSSV nipple

 Displacing the wellbore via CT with suitable method and compatible fluid

 Flowing the well over 96hrs thru different choke sizes while testing integrity and surface sampling

 Retrieving protection sleeve, inject 5 bbl diesel Close TRSSSV, Set BPV in tubing hanger, secure well &amp;amp; release rig.

Note: Detail Clean Up and Well Flowing Program Will Be Issued in Due Time.

5.2 Expected Challenges

5.2.1 26” Section drom surface to 150 m

Challenges

South Azadegan Oilfield Project

Contract No:

F – 20 Well Drilling Program Page 68 of 181

 Complete losses

 Hole cleaning issues due to large hole size

 Bit Blling

Recommendations

 Keep mud weight as low as possible to minimize formation losses.

 Optimize the procedure to fight the losses (see the guide at the end of this mud program) and be

ready with LCM material to mix LCM pill as quick as possible, it is recommended to 8 ppb Mica

M by 8 ppb Mica C to active system from start the Drilling up to 50 mt to prevent the probable

Complete Losses.

 Keep Low GPM from Start drilling to 50 mt to prevent the Probable Complete Losses

 Adequate surface volume should be prepared in advance. A suitable quantitative of Drill water

must be always available on location.

 Do not permit to use The Local Water (Hoor).

 Pump hi-vis pill at each connection to ensure good hole cleaning.

 Maintain adequate viscosity to clean the hole at anticipated penetration rates.

 All solids control equipment should be serviced and brought to optimum operating condition.

 Run all solids control equipment continuously while circulating.

 Utilize the finest mesh screens possible on flow line cleaners.

 Sand trap should be controlled and settled drilled solid should be dumped.

 A final high viscosity sweep should be pumped prior to pulling out of the hole to run casing.

 It is recommended that a high viscosity pill be spotted on bottom prior to running the casing.

 For Get sufficient pre-Hydrate gel its better after Mixing Gel left it on pit at least 6 hours before use.

 The Bentonite should be added slow enough to prevent balling and clogging. The initial yield

depends in part on the quality of the surface equipment. Normally the slurry becomes thicker with

time and agitation.

 The PH should be maintained around 10.5 - 11 with additions of Caustic Soda. This aids in

hydrating the Bentonite, reducing corrosion rates, and minimizing the solubility of contaminants.

 In case of shortage in Drill Water XC‐Polymer HV sweep pill should be pumped just as each

single is drilled, the pill should then be pumped around, allowing at least one lag time before stopping

pumping for connection.

5.2.2 17 ½” Section from 150 m to 2182 m

Challenges

South Azadegan Oilfield Project

Contract No:

F – 20 Well Drilling Program Page 69 of 181

 Hole cleaning issue.

 Possible severe losses.

 Shale

 Marl

 Tight Hole and Hole stability

Recommendations

 It is mandatory to monitor closely the rheological properties in order to ensure adequate hole

cleaning, maximizing the flow rates to assist in cuttings removal.

Poor hole cleaning is indicated by an increase in pump pressure, torque and drag, over-pull at connections and by a lack of an appropriate amount of cuttings on the shakers relative to the ROP and hole size.

 Periodic high viscosity sweeps will help assess the hole cleaning efficiency.

 When Faced with marl lithology must be pump Low Vis pill every single to prevent increase

Rheology unusually. Process of the cutting removing in the Shaker Screens by Mud Engineer

could be the best issue to pump Hi vis pill or Low Vis and Adjust The GPM amount due to have a

good hole cleaning.

 Mud can be treated with additional shale inhibitor if deemed necessary to control shale reactivity

and washouts.

 All the precautions have to be considered in order to take immediate reactions for any risk of

circulation losses: Optimize the procedure to fight the losses (see the guide at the end of this mud

program) and be ready with LCM materials to mix LCM pill as quick as possible.

 This section will be drill up to ±700 mt by Gel mud then Will be displaced by KCL Pol mud

 For Get sufficient pre-Hydrate gel its better after Mixing Gel left it on pit at least 6 hours before

use.

 Test and report key mud properties three times per day. The MBT &amp;amp; Hardness should be tested

and reported 3 times per day.

 Adequate surface volume should be prepared in advance. A suitable quantity of water must be

always available on location.

 All solids control equipment should be serviced and brought to optimum operating condition.

 Also the mud density has to be carefully monitored at 68 pcf at the first then for prevent the tight

hole and hole stability increase the mud weight gradually to 77 pcf .

 Require to maximum effitiency of solid control equipment to control the mud weight

South Azadegan Oilfield Project

Contract No:

F – 20 Well Drilling Program Page 70 of 181

 The shakers should be run with the finest screens possible in

accordance with the flow rate and minimize fluid losses from the shakers by checking deck angle

and running appropriate screens at all times. Also it should be monitored closely to ensure

effective hole cleaning; if there is an inadequate or inconsistent supply of cuttings at the shaker, it

may be necessary to increase the yield point further.

 The mud cleaner should be run with a 200 mesh screen, making sure that the cones are always

clean and discharging heavy liquid. Check the working pressure in order to have the mud cleaner

working at the maximum efficiency.

by discarding the fine solids and consequently minimize the dilution rate.

brown to grey calcareous sandstones, chert debris and gypsum-veined red marl. A fauna of

brackish to freshwater was observed, together with more marine fauna.

Interval Mud Discussion

After drilling shoe track and rate hole with carried Bentonite mud from previous section Salt/KCl/Polymer mud will be employed to drilling this hole section.

Saturated Salt Muds are primarily used to prevent excessive hole enlargement while drilling massive salt beds. They can also be used to reduce dispersion and hydration of shales and clays.

Potassium chloride is the primary source of the potassium ions in this system. In case of soft, sticky red Marl &amp;amp; Clay which encountered problems such as bit balling additions of drilling KCl (3 - 5 %) to inhibit clays in Aghajari is recommended.

Potassium is used in areas where inhibition is required to limit chemical alteration of shales. Potassium performance is based on cationic exchange of potassium for sodium or calcium ions on smectites and interlayered clays. Potassium-based muds perform best on shales containing large quantities of smectite or interlayered clays in the total clay fraction. Shallow shales, containing large amounts of montmorillonite.

Potassium interactions with clay surfaces can be traced to two effects: ionic size and hydration energy. Potassium ions are of the proper size to fit snugly into the spaces between the two silica tetrahedral layers which contact each other in the formation of a three-layer clay packet. The ionic diameter of potassium is 2.66 Å, very close to the available distance of 2.8 Å in the lattice space of the clay structure. A cation slightly smaller than 2.8 Å is desirable to allow for crystalline compaction.

In addition of using KCl, despite Aghajari is an un-permeable formation and seems that isn’t necessary to control Fluid loss, Starch and PAC LV may be used to keep FL under control.

While drilling this section Xanthan gum will be used as base of rheology to extend hole cleaning and providing suitable YP and LSRV. An YP between 15-20 lb/100ft2 for sufficient carrying capacity and a LSRYP at range of 7-15 to preventing any Barite sag in system is required.

As it is seen in geological forecast, soft &amp;amp; sticky marls referred as Gumbo, contained large amount of Smectite and/or Illite could be associated with problems such as bit balling, mud rings, plugged flow lines and hole washout&amp;amp; cause low process of drilling and unnecessary trips and some more difficulties to drill the section as fast as possible. With all those problems reduction of ROP was inevitable, blinding of shaker screens, excessive over pull on trips, washout and stuck pipes has been experienced as well. For problem Solve can add 3-5 % KCl in system.

In case of necessary the inhibition of system can be increased by adding PHPA which adheres to the surface of the drilled cuttings, encapsulating them, and also coating the well bore reducing the hydration of clays in the formation.

South Azadegan Oilfield Project

Contract No:

F – 20 Well Drilling Program Page 77 of 181

Also while drilling this section encounter with Ca2+ based Gypsum is inventible. Gyp is calcium sulfate with water of crystallization (CaSO4.2H2O), Calcium sulfate contamination is similar to cement contamination because both liberate calcium ions, which in turn cause flocculation. Unlike cement, calcium sulfate does not because a PH increase since it supplies a sulfate ion in lieu of a hydroxyl ion. The sulfate ion contributes to flocculation of clay solids, although its effect is small compared to calcium ions. The severity of flocculation depends to a great degree on clay content. When CaSO4 causes the calcium concentration to increase and viscosity may fluctuate drastically. As calcium ion concentrations further increase, a base exchange occurs in which sodium montmorillonite becomes calcium montmorillonite. There are several methods for handling CaSO4 contamination. The drilling fluid can be maintained as a low-calcium fluid by chemically precipitating by adding soda ash.

Interval Mud Discussion

The water-based KCL Polymer system provides effective inhibition when drilling reactive shale’s through below mechanism:

Potassium Chloride provides a source of Potassium ions, which are small enough to fit between the clay platelets without distorting the shale lattice. The Potassium ions are adsorbed on the exchangeable caution sites in the shale lattice and this

South Azadegan Oilfield Project

Contract No:

F – 20 Well Drilling Program Page 82 of 181

holds the platelets together, which helps to minimize clay and shale hydration, swelling and dispersion. A low solids, non-dispersed Salt/KCl/CaCo₃ Polymer drilling fluid is selected for drilling this section. This system is used primarily to drill moderately reactive shale’s. It can be used effectively at temperatures up to 275˚ F – 300˚

If made a decision to run the Glycol System (KCL/Glycol/Polymer mud):

The primary shale inhibition mechanisms in the system are:

1. The cation exchange of potassium ions with the clay to reduce hydration and swelling in conjunction with;

2. A partially hydrolyzed polyacrylamide (PHPA) which adheres to the surface of the drilled cuttings, encapsulating them, and also coating the well bore reducing the hydration of clays in the formation.

3. Clouding out of Glycol: The above methods of shale inhibition from the KCl/PHPA system are enhanced by the clouding effect of the glycol which prevents pore pressure transmission. The stabilization mechanisms combine synergistically to provide inhibition close to that of non-aqueous fluids.

At a specific temperature (cloud point) a water soluble glycol starts to change from soluble to insoluble, forming a thermally activated emulsion (TAME). As the temperature increases the glycol starts to come out of solution and the liquid begins clouding. Eventually the single phase liquid separates into two separate phases.

A: Glycol and water together – at ambient temperature the glycol is 100% water soluble

B: Solution is heated until the glycol reaches ‘cloud point’ and becomes insoluble.

Cloud point is a function of the following variables:

 Salinity of the solution

 Molecular weight and type

 Type of electrolyte

 Concentration of the glycol

Research has concluded that the glycol is associated by hydrogen bonding to the reactive sites of clays. During this adsorption process, water is displaced and ordered structures of glycols are formed. There is little depletion of the glycol from the fluid when drilling, the glycol returning to solution as the cutting moves up the wellbore and the fluid temperature drops below the cloud point. This supports the theory that the bonding between the clay and the glycol is transitory, and there is some mechanism for association and disassociation due to changes in the environment.

South Azadegan Oilfield Project

Contract No:

F – 20 Well Drilling Program Page 83 of 181

It can be concluded that the shale inhibition and formation protection will be achieved by one or both of the following mechanisms:

 The glycol displaces water from adsorption sites on the clay minerals present in shales, especially in the

presence of potassium Ions.

 Blocking the formation pores, preventing further ingress of invasive fluids by clouding out preventing pore

pressure transmission.

During drilling operations, shale cuttings should be monitored continuously for inhibition. If the concentration of inhibitors in the system is insufficient, shale cuttings will be soft and mushy. If the concentration of inhibitors is sufficient, they will retain their integrity. In addition of this controlling API filter press is a key parameter to deal with.

Due to Shale layer in Pabdeh formation different additives such as PHPA and Glycol should be added to active system any prevent any hole problem.

The mud will be formulated and treated to in inhibit and encapsulate the reactive shale found in this area. The PHPA content should be run at 0.25-1 ppb throughout the section. PHPA will be added to the mud on the rig prior to drilling ahead. The success of this system is to achieve and maintain the required concentration of KCL – PHPA and GLYCOL in the system as early as possible in the drilling operation. The main function for the KCL is the primary source of the inhibitive K+ cation the inhibitive property of K+ while drilling reactive shale and clay stone is commonly known and understood. The K+ level derived from the KCL is determined from either historical date or shale characterization and is usually between 3% to 5% KCl in this specific case we would recommend a concentration of ± 11-18 ppb.

5.4 Technical Appendix

5.4.1 Loss Control Procedure

Loss of fluid returns will lower the hydrostatic head of the drilling fluid in the wellbore, thereby inducing a kick. The influx fluid will then flow to the surface or into the zone of lower pressure. Lost circulation can occur in naturally occurring fractured, vuggy, cavernous, sub-normally pressured or pressure depleted formations. Induced losses can occur from mechanical fracturing due to pressure surges while breaking circulation. In all cases of lost circulation, attempts should be made to keep the hole full. The hole can be filled with either light drilling fluid or water. A record of the amount of fluid pumped should be made.

The concentration of LCM will vary according to losses. In the event of seepage losses, treat system with a finer grade of LCM at 20 – 30 Kg/m³. In the event of moderate to high rate of well bore loss, prepare pills at different graded concentrations and spot over thief zone. The concentration may vary between 18 to 70 lb/bbl. In order to avoid LCM plugging MWD tools a circulation sub should be installed in the drill string. The MWD engineer is to advise on the size and concentration of LCM that can be pumped through MWD Tools. Ensure that the drilling displace the LCM pill out of the string prior to shutting down the mud pumps.

Important Note: Please note below concentration and recommended materials may be change with same materials on rig site.

In case of having circulation losses:

Losses less than 10 bbls/hr:

- Active system to be loaded with 10 lb/bbl of Fiber Fine.

Losses 10- 40 bbls/hr:

- Active mud to be loaded with 15- 20 lb/bbl of Fiber Medium.

- Sweep the hole frequently with 50 bbls high viscous pill contains;

- 15 lb/bbl Mica Medium - Corse.

- 10 lb/bbl Walnut Shells Medium -Fine.

- 10 lb/bbl Oyster Shell Fine.

Losses 40 – 100 bbl/hr:

- Stop Drilling.

- Pull out string above the loss zone

- Spot 100 bbls pill contains;

- 30 lb/bbl Fiber coarse.

- 30 lb/bbl Walnut Fine.

- 20 lb/bbl Mica Med.

- Repeat the previous pill minimum of two times.

Losses more than 100 bbls:

- Up to company procedure, may be squeeze 50 bbls of Cement squeeze.

Mixing LCM Pills

South Azadegan Oilfield Project

Contract No:

F – 20 Well Drilling Program Page 92 of 181

The amount of LCM that can be added to a mud depends very much on the mud properties. High gels and YP will help keep the material in suspension. Since LCM is generally of low gradient, excess material tends to float on top if too much is added. The following procedure may prove useful for mixing LCM pills and avoiding the problem of flotation.

1. ENSURE the pill has enough viscosity to keep the low gradient material in suspension before addition of LCM. ADD appropriate viscosifier if required.

2. ADD the material in stages e g. 5, 10, 15, 20 etc. ppb.

3. STOP after desired concentration has been reached, or when it is observed that the material cannot be held in suspension

4. If a higher LCM content is desired, LEAVE the pill to soak for a period of time and then TRY ADDING more material.

- LCM Pill Spotting Procedure

1.After spotting LCM pill, pull the bit above the calculated top of the pill. Wait 30minutes and monitor the annulus.

2.After 30 minutes, attempt to fill the annulus, if not already full. If the hole can be filled, close the BOP and squeeze

10 bbls of LCM pill into the formation without exceeding 200 psi.

3. If the hole remains stable, continue to drill ahead.

4.Should the LCM pill fail to reduce the losses or the hole cannot be filled, then mix and spot another 50 bbls of LCM

pill.

5.Attempt to fill the annulus. If successful, close the BOP and squeeze 20 bbls of LCM pill into the formation

without exceeding 200 psi. If a squeeze pressure develops, hold the pressure for 1 hour before staging the drill

string back to bottom.

Notes:

- All time hole must be full, transfer mud to trip tank and asked driller to fill hole from trip tank.

- All LCM pills must be thoroughly mixed and homogenised before being pumped.

- When pumping an LCM pill through a bit with nozzle smaller than 18/64, DO NOT USED LCM

Medium and Coarse sizes.

- Remove filter screens from the drill pipe and if necessary from the mud pump suction lines.

- This is particularly true if the mud density is high, 14 lb/gal or greater. Fine loss circulation material which

does not adsorb a lot of water should be used in weighted mud.

GUIDELINE FOR FIELD ENGINEERS FOR SHALE INHIBITION

Shale Hydration takes two forms in water-sensitive shales: surface and osmotic adsorption. Surface hydration occurs when a small volume of water is strongly adsorbed onto the planar surfaces of the clays which causes little softening or swelling, but can lead to excessive stresses if the swelling is confined.

Osmotic swelling occurs when a large volume of weakly held water is attracted to the clay surfaces by electrostatic forces. Osmotic swelling causes softening and significant swelling as the adjacent clay layers hydrate water and expand. Osmostic swelling does not generate excessive stresses, even when confined, and can be substantially reduced if Extremely difficult drilling conditions have led to more systematic approaches to analysing wellbore instabilities.

South Azadegan Oilfield Project

Contract No:

F – 20 Well Drilling Program Page 93 of 181

One such approach that can be used as a guideline for the mud engineer involves three basic steps:

1. Monitor and analyse the fundamental failure mechanism.

2. Determine and understand the factors governing this failure mechanism.

3. Model the problem considering impact of proposed changes.

MONITOR AND ANALYZE THE FAILURE MECHANISM

Monitoring of data and events on the rig is the first step of the process and involves:

• Collection, organization and processing of drilling data. Drilling data such as Rate of Penetration (ROP), Revolutions per Minute (RPM), Weight-on-Bit (WOB), Bottom-Hole Assembly (BHA), torque, over pull Trip In Hole (TIH) and Pull Out Of Hole (POOH), swab and surge, flow rate, mud weight, mud Rehology , etc. should be collected, organized and analyzed on a continual basis and compared to the symptoms of wellbore stability being observed. This will help evaluate performance and establish trends or any deviations and measure the effectiveness of treatments and changes.

• Formation characterization. The standard procedure in drilling operations is to apply the knowledge

gained from previous wells to subsequent wells drilled in similar geologic regions. Wellbore-instability

investigation requires evaluation of shales during the drilling process. Since rig site shale testing is limited

due to equipment and time limitations, most evaluations are performed in a properly equipped laboratory.

Laboratory tests are conducted to evaluate shale swelling, dispersibility, cation exchange capacity, hydration capacity, colloidal content, capillary suction time, shale hardness tests and mud compatibility properties.

A number of methods have been used to perform rig site tests. These include tests as simple as the methylene blue test (CEC) measurement of shale; shale hardness measurements; hot-rolled dispersion testing with various mud formulations and additives; and sophisticated analytical measurements of various clay properties. It is particularly important to try and determine the failure mechanism: swelling and softening or brittle spalling. Information from these tests, current shaker observations and mud logger

data are used to evaluate drilling fluid performance, adjust mechanical drilling parameters and making casing design decisions. The primary options to counter shale problems at the rig site are:

• Change the drilling fluid density.

• Change to an oil- or synthetic-base system.

• Change to a more inhibited water-base mud.

• Reduce fluid loss to very low levels and increase filtrate viscosity.

• Utilize pore-plugging additives, emulsified insoluble materials or plastering agents.

• Adjust mechanical drilling parameters.

• Evaluation and analysis of instability symptoms.

Instability warning signs such as the presence of excessive cavings on the shakers for a given ROP, fill on connections, tripping difficulties, torque, stuck pipe, etc. indicate that something is wrong down hole. The magnitude or volume of failed rock should be estimated and recorded with the other drilling parameters. The number and location of specific incidents should be recorded, such as pipe

sticking, fill or packing-off, reaming and re-drilling. All of this information can then be organized and correlated with time and depth to detect the location and quantify the severity of critical sections in the well.

2. DETERMINE AND UNDERSTAND FAILURE MECHANISM

All of the monitored and plotted parameters are then evaluated to identify the most probable mechanism causing the instability. The most useful symptoms used to indicate the mechanism responsible for wellbore instability are:

• Cavings analysis.

• Tripping difficulties.

South Azadegan Oilfield Project

Contract No:

F – 20 Well Drilling Program Page 94 of 181

• Drilling conditions.

• Mud system analysis.

• In-situ conditions.

These symptoms should be evaluated based on an interdisciplinary knowledge of the causes of wellbore

instability to determine the most likely failure mechanism.

3. MODEL AND CONSIDERING PROPOSED CHANGES

Once the monitoring and determination steps have produced parameters, organize and analyze this data to obtain qualitative solutions and evaluate proposed changes. One good way to do this is through the use of a decision tree or flowchart approach to evaluate the possible failure mechanism and to identify the most promising remedies. After arriving at a proposed solution, a corrective measure should be applied and

the results used as feedback into the method and decision tree method.

A decision tree or flowchart, such as shown in Figure 9 for evaluating the cause of excessive cavings, provides a logical path for identification of the mechanism and a qualitative solution. Maintaining hole stability while drilling shale sections can be particularly troublesome. Simple solutions do not always exist, but good drilling practices combined with good mud practices are most often successful. Analysis of the mechanical stress/strain relationships has helped to develop the proper density requirements for hole stability.

5.5 Directional Drilling

DRILLING FLUID PROPERTIES AND SELECTION

It is common knowledge among drilling engineers and drillers that borehole problems can be considerably more severe in a directional hole than in a vertical well. The problems are magnified as the hole angle and horizontal displacement increases. Although most of these reactions are mechanical in nature, much can be done to alleviate them by proper selection and maintenance of the drilling fluid. For example, if a waterbase fluid is being used, lubricants can be added to lower the coefficient of friction between the drill string and borehole or casing. Inhibiting salts can be added to reduce the interaction of the drilling fluid with the exposed formations, thereby improving borehole stability.

There are a number of drilling factors influenced by the drilling fluid, but the following are of primary concern in drilling a horizontal well.

• Borehole instability

• Hole cleaning

• Torque and drag

• Formation damage

• Barite sag

• Hydraulics

Borehole Instability

Borehole instability is one of the more costly, but relatively common problem associated with drilling oil and gas wells. Not only can it impede drilling, it can result in loss of the hole. The term normally conjures thoughts of borehole collapse with accompanying stuck pipe. This is one of the

South Azadegan Oilfield Project

Contract No:

F – 20 Well Drilling Program Page 95 of 181

more critical reactions of borehole instability, but it can manifest itself in more subtle ways such as hole-fill, bridges, hole enlargement, or hole size reduction.

These reactions lead to other associated problems including increased torque and drag, logging difficulties, poor cement jobs, and increased drilling days, all of which add significantly to the drilling cost. It should be pointed out that the discussions to follow do not cover hole enlargement problems from weakly consolidated sands, or rubble zones that erode from the hydraulic action of the drilling fluid.

Stabilization

The swelling activity is controlled by adjusting the electrolyte content of the fluid to minimize expansion of the clays. Lime and gypsum-treated fluids have long been used for this purpose, but basically do not satisfy the inhibition needs of the more troublesome shales. The potassium ion is an effective swelling inhibitor and is used extensively for this purpose through the addition of potassium salts. The concentration of potassium utilized ranges from several hundred mg/L to over 60,000 mg/L. The most cost-effective potassium concentration, however, appears to be in the 3000 to 7000 mg/L range. In marine environments, seawater or seawater with additional sodium chloride, are good alternates to potassium. The tendency for the shale to disperse or subdivide into discrete particles appears to be best controlled by the addition of an adsorptive, high molecular weight water-soluble polymer.

One of the more effective polymers for this purpose is the partially hydrolyzed poly acrylamide with molecular weight in excess of 15 million. These anionic polymers adsorb on to the surface of the cuttings and borehole wall to act as a binder or elastic coating to retard dispersion. Another approach to stabilizing the hard brittle shales that contain natural or induced micro fractures is the use of water-dispersible asphalt or asphaltines. The addition of these type materials appear to plug the micro-fractures, or perhaps even surface pore throats to retard further fluid invasion. This action has proven very effective in certain shales and can be applied in most water base fluids.

Hole Cleaning

Cleaning cuttings from a vertical hole has been covered extensively by numerous investigators. Hole cleaning in a vertical hole is essentially a matter of overcoming the slip velocity of the cuttings with sufficient annular velocity and carrying capacity of the drilling fluid. Although any velocity greater than the settling velocity of the largest cutting will theoretically lift all the cuttings to surface eventually, too low an annular velocity will lead to an undesirable high concentration of cuttings in the annulus. Experience has shown that cuttings concentrations more than 5% by volume cause tight hole or stuck pipe when circulation is stopped.

Cuttings Bed Formation

Radial slip velocity increases with increasing angle of inclination, forcing more cuttings to the low side of the annulus, which eventually results in the formation of a cuttings bed. reported that bed formation was dramatic in the 40° to 50° angle with the bed sliding downward against the flow, resulting in a very high cuttings concentration.

South Azadegan Oilfield Project

Contract No:

F – 20 Well Drilling Program Page 96 of 181

The fact that a cutting bed forms is a serious problem, but the instability of the bed in this critical angle of the well makes the problem even more severe. High torque and drag resulting from the high cutting concentration at the lower part of the angle can obviously result in stuck pipe or loss of circulation.

Hole Cleaning Sweeps

In static drill string concluded that high-density sweeps were more effective than high-density high-viscosity sweeps based on field measurements. The higher viscosity of the latter caused flow diversion to the high side of the wellbore. Not surprisingly, high-viscosity sweeps also performed poorly. Also concluded that the best hole cleaning sweeps were high-density low viscosity sweeps, with a density 3 – 4 ppg higher than that of the drilling fluid. the following procedure is recommended:

• Calculate sweep height in the vertical part of the annulus, and added hydrostatic head in the annulus.

• Rotate at 80+ rpm while pumping the sweep, 180+ rpm is preferred. It is not recommended to pump a weighted sweep while sliding.

• Keep pumping until the sweep is out of the hole. If pumping stops while the sweep is in the

deviated hole, it falls out of the “jet stream” and re-deposits captured fines.

• Avoid increasing the viscosity of the weighted sweep.

• Plan to run 3 – 4 sweeps to achieve desired results when hole cleaning problems are

indicated. One sweep will probably not be sufficient to remedy an existing situation.

• Avoid checking for flow or closing the annulus with the weighted sweep in the drill pipe.

• If desired for preventative maintenance: 1) schedule sweeps every 6 – 8 hours or 500 –

1000 feet (whichever comes first, unless the hole dictates greater frequency); barite/silt

build- ups are dependent on time and footage: and 2) pump a sweep while circulating

bottom up before tripping, and another once back on bottom.

concluded that high-density sweeps were more effective than high-viscosity sweeps.

They strongly advocated the use of sweep reports, which should be standard practice in any drilling fluids operation.

Short Tripping

Another technique that has proven helpful in controlling problems created by the cuttings bed in the high-angle portion of the well is to make periodic short trips. Tripping the bit through the bed not only assures that the bottom hole assembly and bit can be pulled through it, but the action should agitate the bed to the point that a portion will slide down the hole and subsequently be picked up when circulation is commenced. The time intervals for these short trips will be determined by the torque and drag conditions that exist in any particular well. Lacking specific well history, a general rule of thumb is to short trip at least once for every 500 feet of new hole.

Drill String Rotation

The industry is in total agreement that drill string rotation improves hole cleaning, especially in hole sizes less than 17 ½”. The general opinion in the industry is that the optimum drill string rotation rate is approximately 120 rpm. It is believed that the drill string rotation improves hole cleaning by mechanically disturbing the cuttings bed on the low side of the hole. There could also be effects due to skewing the velocity profile in the wellbore and the creation of Taylor Vortices. Encouraged the use of rotary steerable systems.

Turbulence

South Azadegan Oilfield Project

Contract No:

F – 20 Well Drilling Program Page 97 of 181

Bottom hole assembly design becomes important because the flow restrictions of some of the components, such as the measurement-while-drilling tools or positive displacement motors, may not allow sufficient flow to reach turbulence in the annulus. Turbulence can, of course, be induced at some constant flow rate by decreasing the annular area. This may be more difficult to accomplish in a horizontal well because of limitations on the design of drill strings and tool assemblies. An increase in the effective viscosity of the drilling fluid will decrease the Reynolds Number, and thus increase the flow rate required to obtain turbulent flow. Thus, a lower effective viscosity fluid may be desirable in the horizontal well, but attention must also be given to cleaning the larger diameter portion of the upper hole or possible washed-out sections where it is impractical to maintain turbulent flow.

It is interesting to point out a basic fact between static fluid pressure and dynamic fluid pressure. Static fluid pressure is a function of true vertical depth, while dynamic fluid pressure, or ECD, is a function of measured depth. Thus, the ECD will continue to increase, albeit slowly, even after the hole becomes essentially horizontal. The fracture pressure could be reached if the hole was extended to sufficient depth and the fluid density is close to the fracture gradient.

Hole Cleaning Guidelines

The single most important factor related to hole cleaning in deviated wells is flow rate. During directional drilling operations drilled cuttings will settle on the low side of the hole and form a stationary bed if insufficient annular fluid velocity is used. The critical flow rate required to prevent cuttings bed formation must be determined .

Typically few hole cleaning problems exist in vertical or horizontal sections. Most problems

associated with hole cleaning are seen on deviated wells and occur in the 40 – 60 degree section where gravity effects can cause cuttings beds to slump down the hole.Typical flow rates to aim for in ERD wells:

Hole Size Typical Flow Rates17 ½” 800 gpm minimum. Some rigs achieve 850 – 1000 gpm.12 ¼” Aim for 800 gpm (although 800 – 1000 gpm is typically achieved). If 800 gpm is not achievable, ensure tripping procedures are in place for poorly cleaned hole.8 ½” Aim for 400 gpm.

When correctly designed, both laminar and turbulent flow regimes will effectively clean a deviated well. In general increasing the viscosity of a fluid in laminar flow will improve hole cleaning as will a reduction of the viscosity of a fluid in turbulent flow. It is important that one or other regime is selected and that the transition zone between the two is avoided.

Generally viscous fluids in laminar flow are preferred because:

• It is possible to achieve higher cleaning capacity.

• Viscous fluids give better transport in the near-vertical sections.

• Viscous fluids have better suspension characteristics when circulation is stopped.

• It is difficult to achieve “turbulent flow” except in small hole sizes.

Experience has shown that good drilling fluid rheological properties are extremely important to hole cleaning when drilling a high angle well. Studies show that the effects of drilling fluid

South Azadegan Oilfield Project

Contract No:

F – 20 Well Drilling Program Page 98 of 181

rheological properties and annular flow regime are mutually dependent. In the laminar flow regime, increasing fluid viscosity will improve hole cleaning and this is particularly effective if the Yield Stress is high. In the turbulent regime, however, reducing fluid viscosity will help removing cuttings. Therefore the drilling fluid rheological properties should be designed to avoid the transitional flow regime. For hole sizes above 8 ½”, the annular flow is laminar under most circumstances. Therefore it is necessary to specify a minimum Yield Stress. The optimum level required is best established based on field data and experience.

A higher ROP requires a higher flow rate to clean the hole. It is good practice to drill the hole with a steady ROP and select the required flow rate for hole cleaning accordingly. Before making a connection, the hole should be circulated at the normal flow rate to clear the cuttings from around the BHA. Depending upon the hole angle and length of BHA, a circulation time of 5 to 10 minutes is often required.

Before tripping out, the hole should be circulated at the normal flow rate until the shakers are clean, and the drill pipe be rotated at maximum speed/reciprocated in the meantime. This may require up to 3 bottoms-ups, depending on the hole angle and hole size. Below are listed the recommended number of bottoms-up prior to tripping.
